subject: identity verification data pipeline at [COMPANY]
text:
Hi [NAME],

We've been working with Veriff and a large global IDV platform on similar
identity verification use cases as [COMPANY] so I thought I'd reach out.

ML leads in the identity verification space come to us when:

   - New deepfake generation tools release publicly and the eval benchmark
   goes stale faster than the annotation pipeline can refresh it
   - Adding a new geography or document type surfaces model
   underperformance and the path from finding that gap to labelled training
   examples takes weeks, not days
   - The data infrastructure inherited from an earlier product phase wasn't
   built for multimodal sessions with document images, liveness video, and
   face match data in one task

Do you face similar issues at [COMPANY]?

If so, it might be worth having an initial conversation to see whether our
offerings fit your needs.

subject: [COMPANY] Vision at Mount Sinai
text:
Hi [NAME], 

 We work with Iterative Scopes and Proximie on the data layer for clinical video AI.  

 The Mount Sinai partnership caught my attention. Eight hospitals and 100,000 procedures is a significant production milestone. 

 Teams moving into computer vision whilst scaling clinical AI come to us when: 

 - Each new hospital site introduces OR environments the model hasn't seen. 

 - Precision degradation at a flagship customer is a commercial risk before it's a technical one 

 - The data infrastructure that proved the product in a pilot wasn't built to support the retraining cadence a new production deployment requires 

 Do you face similar issues at [COMPANY]? 

 If so, it might be worth having an initial conversation to see whether our offerings fit your needs. I'm free this Thursday if that works.

subject: 83% real-time, 95% in a day: the review layer behind it
text:

We just started working with a top-three US payer and Highmark Health on
the same prior-auth and clinical-document review work [COMPANY] is scaling, so
I thought I'd reach out.

Heads of Clinical AI at payers come to us when:

   - The model produces a prior-auth recommendation and nurses still
   validate it against the source record by hand, so the review cannot keep
   pace with real-time approval volume
   - The speed numbers are public but the auditable record of which
   clinician reviewed which decision does not yet survive a compliance review
   - The team that built the model ends up building the review and
   evaluation tooling too, which pulls engineers off the roadmap

Do you face similar issues at [COMPANY]?

If so, it might be worth an initial conversation to see whether our
offerings fit your needs.

subject: One surgeon, two rooms - the data layer
text:
Hi [NAME],

Yossi's post in February describes the end goal: one surgeon on a complex
decompression in Room A, Dynamis executing routine bone milling
autonomously in Room B. More patients treated, same surgical workforce.

Getting there means training a new autonomous capability for every new
procedure step. Each one needs an annotated operating room video from real
cases. That annotation step sits between every completed procedure and
every new training run.

The pattern we see at teams your size: the engineers building the models
are also manually deciding what to annotate. At 10 cases a month, it is
fine, but at 50 it becomes the bottleneck.

We work with Moon Surgical on exactly this & I thought it would be worth a
20-minute call next Thursday afternoon? Let me know.

subject: the model that supports 100m patients, and the review layer behind it
text:
Hi [NAME],  

 eviCore's stated mission is getting patients the right care faster through evidence-based decisions.  

 The risk is the gap between that mission and what the AI actually does. When a model recommends denial and no clinician trail exists to show the recommendation was reviewed against the source record, the mission becomes very hard to defend, to regulators, to a jury, and to the patients you serve. 

 We work with a large US health-services team on exactly the layer that closes that gap: nurses review LLM output against source clinical records inside their own cloud, every correction is captured, every routing decision is traceable, and the model learns from what it got wrong. 

 With eviCore under strategic review and CMS deadlines six months out, that audit trail isn't a nice-to-have. 

 Is this something your team is actively building?

subject: radiologist correction loop in Pi
text:
Hi [NAME],

I saw the Prostate Intelligence update, the accept-or-revise workflow that
lets radiologists adjust segmentations before sending to PACS. That
human-in-the-loop correction pipeline is the same workflow we use with
another cardiovascular imaging company. Specifically, a DICOM annotation
layer where clinicians can review, adjust, and approve model outputs, with
every correction feeding a traceable retraining record.

The interesting question is what happens to the corrections after they
leave the accept-or-revise step & whether that data is being captured as
labelled ground truth for the next model update, or whether it's lost once
it hits PACS.

Would love to discuss further and how we've helped a similar team and
AbbVie if you have some time later this week. I'm free on Wednesdays and
Thursdays!

subject: Radiologist segmentation corrections at scale
text:
Hi [NAME],

I saw the Prostate Intelligence update, the accept-or-revise workflow that
lets radiologists adjust segmentations before sending to PACS. That
human-in-the-loop correction pipeline is the same workflow we use with
AbbVie.

We work with ML engineers on capturing that kind of correction loop as
labelled training data, with inter-annotator agreement records and audit
trail output built in, rather than letting corrections disappear once they
hit PACS.

The question is whether those radiologist edits are being stored as ground
truth for the next model update or written off once the report leaves.

Let me know if any of that resonates, and would be happy to chat further!

subject: One surgeon, two ORs - what sits between now and that outcome
text:
Hi [NAME],

You have described the end state clearly: one surgeon as the cognitive
orchestrator and a surgical humanoid executing the physically demanding
steps autonomously in a parallel room. More patients are treated with the
same workforce. A healthcare system that does not collapse under
demographic pressure.

The second 510(k) clearance is proof the architecture works. The question
is what determines how fast Dynamis gets from two cleared capabilities to
the ten or twenty that make the parallel operating room model viable at
scale.

Every new autonomous capability requires training data from real cases. The
speed at which that data moves from an operating room procedure into a
validated training run determines how fast the product roadmap moves. We
work with Moon Surgical on exactly that layer, keeping FDA training and
test programmes running in parallel inside one platform rather than two.

Worth 20 minutes to talk about how that compounds for LEM? Please let me
know.

subject: Is your eval layer as strong as your engagement stat?
text:
Hi [NAME],

From the research I've done, [COMPANY]'s agent teams close care gaps, verify coverage, and book appointments in one coordinated workflow.

The agentic AI infrastructure is strong. The gap most teams in this position hit is the human review layer, a systematic way to catch agent output errors before they reach members, and an audit trail that satisfies payer compliance requirements.

We work with healthcare and enterprise AI teams on that layer, including Appfolio and Synthesia on text and document workflows.

Without it:

• 
Agent failures compound silently before member impact.

• 
Payer audits surface gaps in model output traceability.

Worth 20 minutes this week to show what that setup looks like?
